client: I've been really struggling lately with this new job I started at a tech startup about a month ago. The hours are just insane — I'm staying late almost every night, and by the time I get home I'm completely drained, but then I can't even sleep because my mind is still racing about everything I didn't finish. I'm not sure talking about it is actually going to change anything, since the workload isn't going to magically disappear, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It means a lot that you gave this a shot, even with some doubt about whether it would help — that kind of honesty is actually a really good starting point. What you're describing sounds genuinely exhausting, caught in that painful loop where work drains you but then won't let your mind rest enough to recover. I'm curious — when your mind is racing at night, what kinds of thoughts tend to show up most often?

client: Mostly it's like a mental checklist that won't stop running — I keep replaying things I said in meetings, wondering if I came across as incompetent, or mentally cataloging everything that's still unfinished. There's this constant low-level fear that I'm already falling behind and people are starting to notice I might not be cut out for this role. It's like even when my body is done, my brain is still at the office trying to fix everything.
therapist: That image of your brain staying at the office while your body is home is such a vivid way to describe it, and it really captures how relentless that feels. I'm noticing there are two things tangled together here — the worry about unfinished tasks, and this deeper fear that others see you as incompetent — and that second one sounds like it carries a lot of weight. When that fear shows up, like the thought "people are noticing I'm not cut out for this," what actual evidence have you seen at work that supports that belief?

client: Honestly, when I try to think of concrete evidence, it's mostly... vague stuff. Like my manager didn't respond to my last email very enthusiastically, or a colleague seemed distracted during a meeting where I was presenting. I know that sounds thin when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels completely convincing, like those small things are proof of something bigger.
therapist: It's actually a really important insight that you noticed how thin the evidence feels when you say it out loud — that gap between how convincing a thought feels in the moment versus how it holds up under examination is something CBT calls the difference between emotional reasoning and factual reasoning. A distracted colleague or a brief email reply could have dozens of explanations that have nothing to do with your performance, yet your mind is treating them as confirmation of a fear that was already there. What do you think it would take for you to feel genuinely secure in a new role — is there a version of "enough evidence" that would actually satisfy that fear, or does the bar tend to keep moving?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, because honestly I think the bar does keep moving. Like, if my manager gave me positive feedback tomorrow, I'd probably spend the next day worrying that they were just being nice or didn't really mean it. It's uncomfortable to admit that, because it suggests the problem isn't really about the job at all — it's something I'm carrying around with me.
therapist: That realization — that the anxiety might be something you're carrying rather than something the job is doing to you — is genuinely one of the most important and courageous things a person can recognize, even if it feels uncomfortable. It suggests that no amount of external validation will ever fully quiet that inner critic, because it's learned to discount the evidence that doesn't fit its story. I'm wondering, does this feeling of never quite being "enough" feel familiar to you from other areas of your life, or did it show up more with work?

client: Yeah, it's definitely not just work — I think I've always been like this, where I'm waiting for someone to figure out that I'm not as capable as they think I am. It showed up in school, in friendships, even in relationships where I'd convince myself the other person would eventually lose interest once they really got to know me. I guess I just thought getting a "real" job and proving myself professionally would finally make it go away, but it sounds like that was never really the plan my brain had.
therapist: What you're describing — this sense of waiting to be "found out" — is something called impostor phenomenon, and it's remarkably common among capable, self-aware people, which actually makes a lot of sense given how you're able to reflect on it so clearly right now. The painful part is what you've just spotted yourself: that you've been outsourcing the solution to external things like job titles or relationship milestones, hoping they'd fix something that lives on the inside. I'm curious — now that you can see this pattern stretching across so many areas of your life, what do you think it would feel like to relate to yourself with even just a little of the generosity you'd probably offer a close friend in the same situation?

client: Honestly, the idea sounds really appealing in theory, but when I actually try to imagine talking to myself the way I'd talk to a friend, there's this immediate resistance — like my brain says "yeah but a friend deserves that, you actually need to be held accountable." I think part of me genuinely believes that if I stop being hard on myself, I'll just... fall apart or stop trying altogether. It's like the self-criticism feels functional, even though I can see it's also making me miserable.
therapist: That belief — that self-criticism is the thing keeping you functional — is so common, and it makes complete sense that your brain would hold onto it tightly if it feels like a survival strategy. But it's worth gently questioning: in the past month of being really hard on yourself, has it actually made you more productive and at peace, or has it mostly just added suffering on top of the already real demands of the job? What if the self-criticism isn't the engine driving your effort, but actually more like a tax you're paying on top of it?

client: That "tax" framing actually lands differently than I expected — like, when I'm honest with myself, the self-criticism hasn't made me finish more tasks or sleep better, it's just made everything feel heavier and more desperate. But I think my worry is that self-compassion sounds a lot like letting myself off the hook, and I genuinely don't know what it would look like in practice at 11pm when I'm lying awake cataloging my failures. It feels like understanding the concept is one thing, but I have no idea how to actually interrupt that spiral in the moment.
therapist: It's such an important distinction you're drawing — understanding something intellectually and knowing how to use it at 11pm when your nervous system is in full alarm mode are genuinely different skills, and it makes sense you'd need something concrete rather than just a concept. One small experiment worth trying: when the mental checklist starts, see if you can ask yourself "would I say this to a friend on their first month of a hard new job?" — not to dismiss the thoughts, but just to create a tiny pause between the thought and the spiral, like a speed bump rather than a roadblock. What do you think gets in the way most in that moment — is it that the thoughts feel too urgent to slow down, or more that there's a part of you that isn't quite ready to let them go?

client: I think it's honestly both, but if I had to pick one, there's definitely a part of me that isn't ready to let the thoughts go — like some part of me believes that if I keep reviewing everything long enough, I'll somehow fix it or prepare myself for whatever bad thing is coming. The "would I say this to a friend" question is simple enough that I could probably remember it, but I'm a little skeptical that one question is going to cut through when the anxiety is really loud. I guess I'm willing to try it, but I want to be honest that I'm not super confident it'll work.
therapist: Your skepticism is completely fair and actually healthy — one question probably won't silence loud anxiety overnight, and I'd rather you go in with realistic expectations than feel like you've failed if it doesn't work perfectly the first time. What the question is really designed to do isn't fix the anxiety but just create a tiny crack in the certainty that the spiral is useful, and even a small crack repeated over time can start to shift things. I'm also curious about something you said — that part of you believes if you review everything long enough you'll somehow "prepare for whatever bad thing is coming" — what do you imagine that bad thing actually is, if it ever arrived?

client: When I really sit with that question, I think the bad thing is getting fired and having it confirm everything I already suspect about myself — that I was never actually qualified and everyone finally figured it out. And underneath that there's something even more uncomfortable, which is that if I lose this job, I'll have to face how lonely I already am, because right now work is kind of filling up all the space where a social life or real connections would be. It's weird to realize that the job anxiety might actually be protecting me from noticing how isolated I've become.
therapist: That took real courage to say out loud, and I want to sit with it for a moment — you just uncovered something really significant, that the job anxiety might actually be serving as a distraction from a loneliness that feels even more vulnerable and harder to fix. It makes so much sense that your mind would rather spiral about work performance than face that quieter, deeper ache, because at least work feels like something you can theoretically control. I'm wondering — when you imagine a life where the job anxiety wasn't taking up all that space, what would you most want to be there instead?

client: If I'm being honest, what I'd want is just people — like actual friends I could call without it feeling like an imposition, maybe even someone to come home to eventually. But even saying that out loud makes me feel kind of pathetic, like I should have figured out how to build that by now at my age. And there's a part of me that wonders if I've been using the busyness so long that I've actually forgotten how to connect with people, which is a scarier thought than any work deadline.
therapist: Wanting connection — real, genuine human connection — is one of the most fundamentally human things there is, and there is nothing pathetic about it; the fact that you can name it so clearly actually suggests you haven't forgotten how to connect at all, because this conversation right here is a form of that. I also want to gently push back on the "should have figured this out by now" thought, because that's the same moving goalpost we talked about earlier, just pointed at your personal life instead of your job. What would it mean to you if the busyness wasn't a sign that you've broken something in yourself, but rather a very understandable coping strategy that made sense at the time and that you're now, slowly, ready to look beyond?
